title: The Role of Topical Application of Doxycycline in the Treatment of Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw: A Scoping Review
content: Background: Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw (MRONJ) is a severe complication in patients undergoing antiresorptive (bisphosphonates, denosumab) or antiangiogenic therapies. Characterized by progressive bone destruction, local microbial colonization, and impaired mucosal wound healing, MRONJ presents major clinical challenges. Because local microvascularity in necrotic jawbone is severely compromised, systemic antibiotic delivery alone often fails to achieve adequate tissue concentration at the bone surface, while invasive surgical interventions carry significant morbidity in frail oncology or osteoporotic patients. Objective: To systematically map and synthesize the existing evidence on the biochemical mechanisms, tissue interactions, and theoretical/clinical rationale supporting topical doxycycline application as a conservative management strategy for MRONJ. Methods: A scoping review literature search strategy across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library was established to identify pre-clinical and clinical studies evaluating doxycycline's non-antimicrobial host-modulation properties, chemical substantivity to mineralized tissues, local pharmacokinetics, and clinical outcomes in oral infections and maxillofacial bone necrosis. Results / Synthesis of Evidence: The synthesized evidence reveals three primary mechanisms supporting topical doxycycline: A) Host Modulation via MMP Inhibition: Doxycycline acts as a potent non-antimicrobial inhibitor of matrix metalloproteinases (specifically MMP-8 and MMP-9), suppressing soft-tissue and bone collagen degradation while downregulating osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. B) High Chemical Substantivity: Doxycycline exhibits a high affinity for calcium and hydroxyapatite crystals on exposed bone surfaces. This binding capacity (substantivity) allows for sustained, localized drug release that directly combats polymicrobial biofilms without systemic toxicity. C) Bypass of Vascular Compromise: Topical delivery places high therapeutic concentrations directly onto exposed necrotic voids and bone fistulas, overcoming the pharmacokinetic limitations of compromised regional vascularity. Conclusions: Topical doxycycline represents a scientifically grounded, non-invasive adjunctive modality for MRONJ management. By targeting both surface biofilm colonization and underlying matrix-degrading inflammatory cascades, it provides a compelling theoretical basis for clinical trials investigating conservative, stage-specific therapeutic protocols.
